lessons.title: Claims and Evidence: Applied Research Seminar
lessons.subject: Critical Thinking
learning_objectives: Explain the central concepts and vocabulary of Claims and Evidence.
Apply Claims and Evidence to a worked Critical Thinking problem.
Critically evaluate evidence, assumptions, and alternative conclusions.
lessons.reading_material:
This UG4 lesson examines Claims and Evidence through applied research seminar in Critical Thinking. It establishes the main vocabulary, the relationships between the core ideas, and the boundary conditions under which a claim or method is reliable.

Learners work from a concrete Critical Thinking problem to an evidence-based explanation. They must identify assumptions, distinguish observations from interpretations, and use the supplied source to check important claims. The worked analysis deliberately includes an incomplete argument so that learners can diagnose what evidence is still needed.

The lesson concludes by applying Claims and Evidence to a second context. Learners compare alternatives, justify a decision, record uncertainty, and reflect on how the conclusion might change if the evidence changed. Reference: https://plato.stanford.edu/
practical_activities: Build a concept map for Claims and Evidence.
Complete a source-backed Critical Thinking case analysis.
Compare two possible conclusions and defend the stronger one.

exercises.q: What evidence is most important when applying Claims and Evidence?
exercises.answer: Relevant, credible evidence that directly supports the stated conclusion.

exercises.q: Give one limitation of the worked Critical Thinking case.
exercises.answer: A valid answer identifies a missing assumption, evidence gap, or limit on generalisation.

homework.task: Write a source-backed application of Claims and Evidence to a new case and include one counterargument.

revision.notes: Review the definition, evidence, application, and limitations of Claims and Evidence.
revision.tip: Reconstruct the argument from memory, then verify it against the cited source.

questions.q: Which response best demonstrates mastery of Claims and Evidence?
options: A conclusion supported by relevant evidence and explicit assumptions
A copied definition with no application
questions.answer: A conclusion supported by relevant evidence and explicit assumptions

figure.caption: Key concepts in “Claims and Evidence: Applied Research Seminar”

lessons.subject: Health Education
learning_objectives: Explain the core ideas of capstone study: public health fundamentals at Undergraduate Year 4 depth.
Apply capstone study: public health fundamentals concepts to worked examples and problems.
Critically discuss how capstone study: public health fundamentals connects to real-world practice in health education.
lessons.reading_material:
Capstone Study: Public Health Fundamentals is a capstone-level undergraduate module in Health Education, deepening prior levels with more rigorous theory, worked examples, and assessment matched to Undergraduate Year 4.

Capstone Study: Public Health Fundamentals sits at a point in Health Education where genuine understanding pays off disproportionately: it is referenced, directly or indirectly, in a wide range of subsequent material. Students who treat it as a box to check tend to find themselves relearning it under time pressure later; students who invest in understanding it now tend to find later modules noticeably more tractable.

The intended learning outcomes for this module are: Explain the core ideas of capstone study: public health fundamentals at Undergraduate Year 4 depth; Apply capstone study: public health fundamentals concepts to worked examples and problems; Critically discuss how capstone study: public health fundamentals connects to real-world practice in health education. Treat these less as a checklist and more as a self-assessment tool: after working through the material, try to satisfy each outcome without reference to your notes, and any outcome you cannot satisfy cleanly marks exactly where to focus your remaining study time.

Central terminology for this module: Capstone, Study, Public, Health, Fundamentals. A useful habit at this stage of study is to maintain your own running glossary rather than relying on recognising terms in context; being asked to produce a definition cold, without the surrounding sentence to lean on, is a much better test of whether a concept has actually been internalised.

Students frequently underestimate how much of the difficulty in material like this is conceptual rather than computational: getting the right numeric answer to a problem is not the same as being able to explain, in your own words and without notes, why the method used was appropriate. Assessment at this level increasingly rewards the latter, so it is worth practising explanation, not just calculation, as you work through the material.

To consolidate this module, work through the following: Guided worked example on capstone study: public health fundamentals; Small-group discussion / problem set on capstone study: public health fundamentals. Treat this as a diagnostic as much as an exercise: wherever it exposes a gap in your understanding, that gap is exactly where additional study time is best spent, rather than spreading review evenly across material you have already mastered.

The associated assignment is: Write a short summary connecting capstone study: public health fundamentals to one real-world example. Beyond satisfying the requirement, use it as an opportunity to surface exactly which parts of the module you can apply confidently and which parts you can only recognise -- that distinction is the most useful information you can extract from any assignment.

For review before assessment: Review capstone study: public health fundamentals before moving to the next module. A strong test of readiness is being able to reconstruct the core argument of this module from a blank page, in your own words and without consulting notes; if you can do that fluently, recognition-based review is no longer the most valuable use of your remaining study time.

To close, treat mastery of Capstone Study: Public Health Fundamentals as an ongoing project rather than a one-time task completed when the module ends. The strongest students in any Health Education course are distinguished less by innate ability than by the habit of returning to earlier material once later material makes its relevance clearer -- make a note to revisit this module once you have progressed further in the course.

It is worth situating Capstone Study: Public Health Fundamentals within Health Education before working through the material. Topics at this level are rarely self-contained; Capstone Study: Public Health Fundamentals both depends on concepts introduced earlier in the course and sets up reasoning that later modules will assume you already have available. Treating it as an isolated fact to memorise, rather than a piece of a larger argument, is the single most common reason students find later material harder than it needs to be.

learning_objectives: Explain the core ideas of outbreak investigation methodology at Undergraduate Year 4 depth.
Apply outbreak investigation methodology concepts to worked examples and problems.
Critically discuss how outbreak investigation methodology connects to real-world practice in health education.
lessons.reading_material:
Examines the systematic steps epidemiologists follow to identify the source of a disease outbreak.

A brief note on why Outbreak Investigation Methodology earns a dedicated module in Health Education. At this level, coursework is structured so that each topic does real conceptual work -- it either resolves a limitation of the previous topic, extends it to a broader class of cases, or introduces a method that later topics reuse. Understanding which of these roles Outbreak Investigation Methodology plays will make the rest of the module easier to follow.

The intended learning outcomes for this module are: Explain the core ideas of outbreak investigation methodology at Undergraduate Year 4 depth; Apply outbreak investigation methodology concepts to worked examples and problems; Critically discuss how outbreak investigation methodology connects to real-world practice in health education. Treat these less as a checklist and more as a self-assessment tool: after working through the material, try to satisfy each outcome without reference to your notes, and any outcome you cannot satisfy cleanly marks exactly where to focus your remaining study time.

Central terminology for this module: Outbreak, Investigation, Methodology. A useful habit at this stage of study is to maintain your own running glossary rather than relying on recognising terms in context; being asked to produce a definition cold, without the surrounding sentence to lean on, is a much better test of whether a concept has actually been internalised.

Students frequently underestimate how much of the difficulty in material like this is conceptual rather than computational: getting the right numeric answer to a problem is not the same as being able to explain, in your own words and without notes, why the method used was appropriate. Assessment at this level increasingly rewards the latter, so it is worth practising explanation, not just calculation, as you work through the material.

To consolidate this module, work through the following: Guided worked example on outbreak investigation methodology; Small-group discussion / problem set on outbreak investigation methodology. Treat this as a diagnostic as much as an exercise: wherever it exposes a gap in your understanding, that gap is exactly where additional study time is best spent, rather than spreading review evenly across material you have already mastered.

The associated assignment is: Write a short summary connecting outbreak investigation methodology to one real-world example. Beyond satisfying the requirement, use it as an opportunity to surface exactly which parts of the module you can apply confidently and which parts you can only recognise -- that distinction is the most useful information you can extract from any assignment.

For review before assessment: Review outbreak investigation methodology before moving to the next module. A strong test of readiness is being able to reconstruct the core argument of this module from a blank page, in your own words and without consulting notes; if you can do that fluently, recognition-based review is no longer the most valuable use of your remaining study time.

To close, treat mastery of Outbreak Investigation Methodology as an ongoing project rather than a one-time task completed when the module ends. The strongest students in any Health Education course are distinguished less by innate ability than by the habit of returning to earlier material once later material makes its relevance clearer -- make a note to revisit this module once you have progressed further in the course.

It is worth situating Outbreak Investigation Methodology within Health Education before working through the material. Topics at this level are rarely self-contained; Outbreak Investigation Methodology both depends on concepts introduced earlier in the course and sets up reasoning that later modules will assume you already have available. Treating it as an isolated fact to memorise, rather than a piece of a larger argument, is the single most common reason students find later material harder than it needs to be.

Outbreak Investigation Methodology sits at a point in Health Education where genuine understanding pays off disproportionately: it is referenced, directly or indirectly, in a wide range of subsequent material. Students who treat it as a box to check tend to find themselves relearning it under time pressure later; students who invest in understanding it now tend to find later modules noticeably more tractable.

lessons.reading_material:
This UG4 lesson examines Health Literacy through applied research seminar in Health Education. It establishes the main vocabulary, the relationships between the core ideas, and the boundary conditions under which a claim or method is reliable.

Learners work from a concrete Health Education problem to an evidence-based explanation. They must identify assumptions, distinguish observations from interpretations, and use the supplied source to check important claims. The worked analysis deliberately includes an incomplete argument so that learners can diagnose what evidence is still needed.

The lesson concludes by applying Health Literacy to a second context. Learners compare alternatives, justify a decision, record uncertainty, and reflect on how the conclusion might change if the evidence changed. Reference: https://www.who.int/

lessons.reading_material:
Capstone Study: Networks & Databases is a capstone-level undergraduate module in ICT & Computer Science, deepening prior levels with more rigorous theory, worked examples, and assessment matched to Undergraduate Year 4.

Capstone Study: Networks & Databases sits at a point in ICT & Computer Science where genuine understanding pays off disproportionately: it is referenced, directly or indirectly, in a wide range of subsequent material. Students who treat it as a box to check tend to find themselves relearning it under time pressure later; students who invest in understanding it now tend to find later modules noticeably more tractable.

real_world_examples: How 'Capstone Study: Networks & Databases' shows up in real-world ict & computer science practice: Capstone Study: Networks & Databases is a capstone-level undergraduate module in ICT & Computer Science, deepening prior levels with more rigorous theory, worked examples, and assessment matched to Undergraduate Year 4.

How 'Capstone Study: Computer Science Theory' shows up in real-world ict & computer science practice: Capstone Study: Computer Science Theory extends ICT & Computer Science at Undergraduate Year 4, connecting computer science theory to practical problems, projects, and real-world case studies.
ICT & Computer Science.learning_path: At Undergraduate Year 4, ICT & Computer Science progresses through Capstone Study: Networks & Databases, Capstone Study: Computer Science Theory. Learners should complete modules in order, attempt the quiz after each module, and take the level exam once all modules are complete before advancing to the next level.

lessons.title: Business Purpose: Conceptual Foundations
lessons.subject: Business Studies
learning_objectives: Explain the central concepts and vocabulary of Business Purpose.
Apply Business Purpose to a worked Business Studies problem.
Critically evaluate evidence, assumptions, and alternative conclusions.
lessons.reading_material:
This UG4 lesson examines Business Purpose through conceptual foundations in Business Studies. It establishes the main vocabulary, the relationships between the core ideas, and the boundary conditions under which a claim or method is reliable.

Learners work from a concrete Business Studies problem to an evidence-based explanation. They must identify assumptions, distinguish observations from interpretations, and use the supplied source to check important claims. The worked analysis deliberately includes an incomplete argument so that learners can diagnose what evidence is still needed.

The lesson concludes by applying Business Purpose to a second context. Learners compare alternatives, justify a decision, record uncertainty, and reflect on how the conclusion might change if the evidence changed. Reference: https://openstax.org/details/books/principles-management
practical_activities: Build a concept map for Business Purpose.
Complete a source-backed Business Studies case analysis.
Compare two possible conclusions and defend the stronger one.

exercises.q: What evidence is most important when applying Business Purpose?
exercises.answer: Relevant, credible evidence that directly supports the stated conclusion.

exercises.q: Give one limitation of the worked Business Studies case.
exercises.answer: A valid answer identifies a missing assumption, evidence gap, or limit on generalisation.

homework.task: Write a source-backed application of Business Purpose to a new case and include one counterargument.

revision.notes: Review the definition, evidence, application, and limitations of Business Purpose.
revision.tip: Reconstruct the argument from memory, then verify it against the cited source.

questions.q: Which response best demonstrates mastery of Business Purpose?
options: A conclusion supported by relevant evidence and explicit assumptions
A copied definition with no application
questions.answer: A conclusion supported by relevant evidence and explicit assumptions

figure.caption: Key concepts in “Business Purpose: Conceptual Foundations”

Critically evaluate evidence, assumptions, and alternative conclusions.
lessons.reading_material:
This UG4 lesson examines Public Administration through comparative case study in Civics. It establishes the main vocabulary, the relationships between the core ideas, and the boundary conditions under which a claim or method is reliable.

Learners work from a concrete Civics problem to an evidence-based explanation. They must identify assumptions, distinguish observations from interpretations, and use the supplied source to check important claims. The worked analysis deliberately includes an incomplete argument so that learners can diagnose what evidence is still needed.

The lesson concludes by applying Public Administration to a second context. Learners compare alternatives, justify a decision, record uncertainty, and reflect on how the conclusion might change if the evidence changed. Reference: https://www.un.org/en/about-us/universal-declaration-of-human-rights
practical_activities: Build a concept map for Public Administration.
Complete a source-backed Civics case analysis.
Compare two possible conclusions and defend the stronger one.

exercises.answer: Relevant, credible evidence that directly supports the stated conclusion.

Apply Sustainability Transitions to a worked Environmental Science problem.
Critically evaluate evidence, assumptions, and alternative conclusions.
lessons.reading_material:
This UG4 lesson examines Sustainability Transitions through comparative case study in Environmental Science. It establishes the main vocabulary, the relationships between the core ideas, and the boundary conditions under which a claim or method is reliable.

Learners work from a concrete Environmental Science problem to an evidence-based explanation. They must identify assumptions, distinguish observations from interpretations, and use the supplied source to check important claims. The worked analysis deliberately includes an incomplete argument so that learners can diagnose what evidence is still needed.

The lesson concludes by applying Sustainability Transitions to a second context. Learners compare alternatives, justify a decision, record uncertainty, and reflect on how the conclusion might change if the evidence changed. Reference: https://www.unep.org/resources
practical_activities: Build a concept map for Sustainability Transitions.
Complete a source-backed Environmental Science case analysis.
Compare two possible conclusions and defend the stronger one.

exercises.q: What evidence is most important when applying Sustainability Transitions?
exercises.answer: Relevant, credible evidence that directly supports the stated conclusion.

exercises.q: Give one limitation of the worked Environmental Science case.
exercises.answer: A valid answer identifies a missing assumption, evidence gap, or limit on generalisation.

homework.task: Write a source-backed application of Sustainability Transitions to a new case and include one counterargument.

revision.notes: Review the definition, evidence, application, and limitations of Sustainability Transitions.
revision.tip: Reconstruct the argument from memory, then verify it against the cited source.

questions.q: Which response best demonstrates mastery of Sustainability Transitions?
options: A conclusion supported by relevant evidence and explicit assumptions
A copied definition with no application
questions.answer: A conclusion supported by relevant evidence and explicit assumptions

figure.caption: Key concepts in “Sustainability Transitions: Comparative Case Study”

lessons.subject: World Politics
learning_objectives: Explain the central concepts and vocabulary of Technology and Geopolitics.
Apply Technology and Geopolitics to a worked World Politics problem.
Critically evaluate evidence, assumptions, and alternative conclusions.
lessons.reading_material:
This UG4 lesson examines Technology and Geopolitics through evidence and data in World Politics. It establishes the main vocabulary, the relationships between the core ideas, and the boundary conditions under which a claim or method is reliable.

Learners work from a concrete World Politics problem to an evidence-based explanation. They must identify assumptions, distinguish observations from interpretations, and use the supplied source to check important claims. The worked analysis deliberately includes an incomplete argument so that learners can diagnose what evidence is still needed.

The lesson concludes by applying Technology and Geopolitics to a second context. Learners compare alternatives, justify a decision, record uncertainty, and reflect on how the conclusion might change if the evidence changed. Reference: https://www.un.org/en/global-issues
practical_activities: Build a concept map for Technology and Geopolitics.
Complete a source-backed World Politics case analysis.
Compare two possible conclusions and defend the stronger one.

exercises.q: What evidence is most important when applying Technology and Geopolitics?
exercises.answer: Relevant, credible evidence that directly supports the stated conclusion.

exercises.q: Give one limitation of the worked World Politics case.
exercises.answer: A valid answer identifies a missing assumption, evidence gap, or limit on generalisation.

homework.task: Write a source-backed application of Technology and Geopolitics to a new case and include one counterargument.

revision.notes: Review the definition, evidence, application, and limitations of Technology and Geopolitics.
revision.tip: Reconstruct the argument from memory, then verify it against the cited source.

questions.q: Which response best demonstrates mastery of Technology and Geopolitics?
options: A conclusion supported by relevant evidence and explicit assumptions
A copied definition with no application
questions.answer: A conclusion supported by relevant evidence and explicit assumptions

figure.caption: Key concepts in “Technology and Geopolitics: Evidence and Data”

Apply Religious Ethics to a worked World Religions problem.
Critically evaluate evidence, assumptions, and alternative conclusions.
lessons.reading_material:
This UG4 lesson examines Religious Ethics through worked analysis in World Religions. It establishes the main vocabulary, the relationships between the core ideas, and the boundary conditions under which a claim or method is reliable.

Learners work from a concrete World Religions problem to an evidence-based explanation. They must identify assumptions, distinguish observations from interpretations, and use the supplied source to check important claims. The worked analysis deliberately includes an incomplete argument so that learners can diagnose what evidence is still needed.

The lesson concludes by applying Religious Ethics to a second context. Learners compare alternatives, justify a decision, record uncertainty, and reflect on how the conclusion might change if the evidence changed. Reference: https://pluralism.org/religions
practical_activities: Build a concept map for Religious Ethics.
Complete a source-backed World Religions case analysis.
Compare two possible conclusions and defend the stronger one.

exercises.q: What evidence is most important when applying Religious Ethics?
exercises.answer: Relevant, credible evidence that directly supports the stated conclusion.

exercises.q: Give one limitation of the worked World Religions case.
exercises.answer: A valid answer identifies a missing assumption, evidence gap, or limit on generalisation.

homework.task: Write a source-backed application of Religious Ethics to a new case and include one counterargument.

revision.notes: Review the definition, evidence, application, and limitations of Religious Ethics.
revision.tip: Reconstruct the argument from memory, then verify it against the cited source.

questions.q: Which response best demonstrates mastery of Religious Ethics?
options: A conclusion supported by relevant evidence and explicit assumptions
A copied definition with no application
questions.answer: A conclusion supported by relevant evidence and explicit assumptions

figure.caption: Key concepts in “Religious Ethics: Worked Analysis”

lessons.reading_material:
This module offers a comparative look at how it connects to neighbouring mythologies of Hindu Mythology, the body of myth, belief, and religious practice that developed in the Indian subcontinent.

Studying Hindu Mythology matters for reasons beyond entertainment value: myth was, for the people of the Indian subcontinent, a working framework for explaining natural phenomena, justifying social and political order, and transmitting moral and religious values across generations. A careful student learns to read these stories the way the original audience encountered them -- as meaningful, structured accounts of the world, not as simple children's tales.

Among the most significant figures are: Brahma, the creator god, one of the Trimurti (trinity) alongside Vishnu and Shiva; Vishnu, the preserver god, believed to descend to Earth in avatars including Rama and Krishna to restore cosmic order (dharma); Shiva, the destroyer and transformer god, often depicted meditating on Mount Kailash or dancing as Nataraja; Devi (the Goddess), worshipped in forms including Durga, Kali, Lakshmi (goddess of wealth), and Saraswati (goddess of knowledge); Ganesha, the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati, worshipped as the remover of obstacles.

The tradition's cosmology describes that the universe undergoes endless cycles of creation, preservation, and destruction (Brahma creating, Vishnu preserving, Shiva destroying), and different texts describe creation emerging from a cosmic ocean or from the sound 'Om'. It is also worth asking what social or historical circumstance the account may reflect, since myth often encodes real concerns of the society that told it. This detail is among the better-documented parts of the tradition, thanks to surviving texts, inscriptions, or archaeological evidence. Later artists, writers, and, in some cases, entire religious movements have returned to this element repeatedly across the centuries. This is worth dwelling on, since it shows how a mythological system organizes explanation, morality, and meaning for the people who held it.

Its legendary narratives include: The Ramayana, an epic attributed to the sage Valmiki, follows Prince Rama's quest to rescue his wife Sita from the demon king Ravana; The Mahabharata, one of the longest epic poems in world literature, recounts the Kurukshetra War between the Pandava and Kaurava families and includes the Bhagavad Gita, a philosophical dialogue between the prince Arjuna and the god Krishna; Krishna, an avatar of Vishnu, appears throughout Hindu mythology as both a mischievous youth and a wise divine teacher; Hanuman, the monkey-god devoted to Rama, is celebrated for his strength, loyalty, and role in the Ramayana. Later artists, writers, and, in some cases, entire religious movements have returned to this element repeatedly across the centuries. This is worth dwelling on, since it shows how a mythological system organizes explanation, morality, and meaning for the people who held it. Read alongside the tradition's other elements, it forms part of a coherent worldview rather than an isolated tale. Students encountering this for the first time should note how specific and structured the account is, rather than a vague or arbitrary story.

What is known of its ritual life and key texts includes: The Vedas, composed over roughly a thousand years beginning around 1500 BCE, are the oldest surviving Hindu scriptures, including hymns, rituals, and philosophy; The Puranas are a large body of later texts recounting the genealogies, deeds, and legends of the gods; Temple worship (puja), pilgrimage to sacred sites such as Varanasi, and major festivals including Diwali (festival of lights) and Holi (festival of colors) remain central living practices. Read alongside the tradition's other elements, it forms part of a coherent worldview rather than an isolated tale. Students encountering this for the first time should note how specific and structured the account is, rather than a vague or arbitrary story. Comparative mythologists have long noted how this connects to patterns found in other, geographically distant traditions -- a useful reminder that human cultures have repeatedly reached for similar kinds of explanation. It is also worth asking what social or historical circumstance the account may reflect, since myth often encodes real concerns of the society that told it.

Modern culture continues to draw on it through: Hindu mythology has directly shaped the art, temple architecture, classical dance, and literature of South and Southeast Asia for over two thousand years; Major Hindu temple complexes, including Angkor Wat in Cambodia, were built to honor Vishnu and later repurposed for Buddhist worship, showing the tradition's reach across Southeast Asia; Hindu mythological figures and stories remain central to contemporary Indian cinema, television, and popular festivals. Comparative mythologists have long noted how this connects to patterns found in other, geographically distant traditions -- a useful reminder that human cultures have repeatedly reached for similar kinds of explanation. It is also worth asking what social or historical circumstance the account may reflect, since myth often encodes real concerns of the society that told it. This detail is among the better-documented parts of the tradition, thanks to surviving texts, inscriptions, or archaeological evidence. Later artists, writers, and, in some cases, entire religious movements have returned to this element repeatedly across the centuries.

No single module can cover every surviving story and variant of Hindu Mythology, but the elements above -- its deities, its account of origins, its heroes, its practice, and its legacy -- give a structured foundation for further study of one of the richest mythological traditions to survive from the Indian subcontinent.

This module offers a comparative look at how it connects to neighbouring mythologies of African Mythology, the body of myth, belief, and religious practice that developed in the diverse cultures of the African continent.

Studying African Mythology matters for reasons beyond entertainment value: myth was, for the people of the diverse cultures of the African continent, a working framework for explaining natural phenomena, justifying social and political order, and transmitting moral and religious values across generations. A careful student learns to read these stories the way the original audience encountered them -- as meaningful, structured accounts of the world, not as simple children's tales.

Among the most significant figures are: Olodumare (also called Olorun), the supreme creator god in Yoruba religious tradition of West Africa; Anansi, the trickster spider figure of Akan (Ghanaian) mythology, renowned for cleverness and storytelling; Amma, the creator god of Dogon mythology in Mali; Mawu-Lisa, a dual moon-and-sun creator deity in Fon and Ewe mythology of West Africa (Benin, Togo).

The tradition's cosmology describes that African mythological traditions vary enormously across the continent's thousands of distinct cultures; in Yoruba tradition, the god Obatala was sent by Olodumare to create solid land from the primordial waters and to shape the first human beings from clay, while other regional traditions describe entirely different creation narratives suited to their own peoples and landscapes. It is also worth asking what social or historical circumstance the account may reflect, since myth often encodes real concerns of the society that told it. This detail is among the better-documented parts of the tradition, thanks to surviving texts, inscriptions, or archaeological evidence. Later artists, writers, and, in some cases, entire religious movements have returned to this element repeatedly across the centuries. This is worth dwelling on, since it shows how a mythological system organizes explanation, morality, and meaning for the people who held it.

Its legendary narratives include: Anansi the spider is one of the most widely known trickster figures in world mythology, using wit rather than strength to outsmart more powerful beings, and his stories spread with the transatlantic slave trade to become foundational to Caribbean and African American folklore as well; Sundiata Keita, founder of the Mali Empire in the 13th century, became a legendary hero-king whose life is recounted in the Epic of Sundiata, a foundational oral epic of West Africa still performed by griot storytellers today; Shaka Zulu, the early 19th-century Zulu king, became a major figure of Southern African historical legend for his military reforms and the rise of the Zulu Kingdom. Later artists, writers, and, in some cases, entire religious movements have returned to this element repeatedly across the centuries. This is worth dwelling on, since it shows how a mythological system organizes explanation, morality, and meaning for the people who held it. Read alongside the tradition's other elements, it forms part of a coherent worldview rather than an isolated tale. Students encountering this for the first time should note how specific and structured the account is, rather than a vague or arbitrary story.

What is known of its ritual life and key texts includes: Because most African mythological traditions were preserved primarily through oral transmission, professional oral historians and storytellers -- griots in West Africa in particular -- have historically played a central role in preserving and transmitting myth, genealogy, and history together; Yoruba religious tradition, including belief in the orishas (deities/spirits), spread with the transatlantic slave trade and directly shaped syncretic religions in the Americas, including Santeria in Cuba and Candomble in Brazil; Ancestor veneration and belief in a spirit world closely connected to the living are common, though far from universal, threads across many distinct African mythological and religious traditions. Read alongside the tradition's other elements, it forms part of a coherent worldview rather than an isolated tale. Students encountering this for the first time should note how specific and structured the account is, rather than a vague or arbitrary story. Comparative mythologists have long noted how this connects to patterns found in other, geographically distant traditions -- a useful reminder that human cultures have repeatedly reached for similar kinds of explanation. It is also worth asking what social or historical circumstance the account may reflect, since myth often encodes real concerns of the society that told it.

Modern culture continues to draw on it through: Anansi stories remain widely told across West Africa and the Caribbean today, and directly shaped later African American folklore traditions such as the Br'er Rabbit stories; Yoruba-derived religious traditions remain actively practiced by millions of people across the Americas today, particularly in Cuba, Brazil, and parts of the United States; African mythological and oral epic traditions, including the Epic of Sundiata, remain the subject of active scholarly study and continue to be performed by griots in West Africa today. Comparative mythologists have long noted how this connects to patterns found in other, geographically distant traditions -- a useful reminder that human cultures have repeatedly reached for similar kinds of explanation. It is also worth asking what social or historical circumstance the account may reflect, since myth often encodes real concerns of the society that told it. This detail is among the better-documented parts of the tradition, thanks to surviving texts, inscriptions, or archaeological evidence. Later artists, writers, and, in some cases, entire religious movements have returned to this element repeatedly across the centuries.

No single module can cover every surviving story and variant of African Mythology, but the elements above -- its deities, its account of origins, its heroes, its practice, and its legacy -- give a structured foundation for further study of one of the richest mythological traditions to survive from the diverse cultures of the African continent.

This module offers a comparative look at how it connects to neighbouring mythologies of Other World Mythologies (Slavic, Native American, and Australian Aboriginal), the body of myth, belief, and religious practice that developed in Eastern Europe, the Americas, and Australia.

A careful student learns to read these stories the way the original audience encountered them -- as meaningful, structured accounts of the world, not as simple children's tales.

Among the most significant figures are: Perun, the Slavic god of thunder and the sky, considered the chief deity in the pre-Christian religion of the Eastern Slavs; Coyote, a widespread trickster and creator figure appearing across many distinct Native American mythological traditions, particularly in the western United States; The Rainbow Serpent, a major creator being found across many Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime traditions, associated with water sources and the shaping of the landscape; Baiame, a sky-father creator figure central to the Dreaming traditions of several Aboriginal peoples of southeastern Australia.

The tradition's cosmology describes that each of these traditions has its own distinct account: Slavic myth describes a cosmic struggle between Perun (order/sky) and Veles (chaos/underworld); many Native American traditions describe an 'Earth-Diver' creation, in which an animal dives to the bottom of a primordial ocean to retrieve mud that becomes land; and Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime accounts describe ancestral beings shaping the landscape's rivers, mountains, and rock formations during a foundational creative period. It is also worth asking what social or historical circumstance the account may reflect, since myth often encodes real concerns of the society that told it. This detail is among the better-documented parts of the tradition, thanks to surviving texts, inscriptions, or archaeological evidence. Later artists, writers, and, in some cases, entire religious movements have returned to this element repeatedly across the centuries. This is worth dwelling on, since it shows how a mythological system organizes explanation, morality, and meaning for the people who held it.

Its legendary narratives include: In Slavic mythology, Baba Yaga, an ambiguous witch-like figure living in a hut on chicken legs, appears throughout Russian and broader Slavic folklore, sometimes as a villain and sometimes as an unlikely helper; Native American trickster-hero figures, including Coyote, Raven (in Pacific Northwest traditions), and Iktomi (in Lakota tradition), use cunning to shape the world and teach moral lessons, often through their own mistakes and misadventures; Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime narratives describe ancestral beings whose journeys across the land during the creative period are believed to have physically shaped specific landmarks, with those same routes preserved today as 'songlines' passed down through generations. Later artists, writers, and, in some cases, entire religious movements have returned to this element repeatedly across the centuries. This is worth dwelling on, since it shows how a mythological system organizes explanation, morality, and meaning for the people who held it. Read alongside the tradition's other elements, it forms part of a coherent worldview rather than an isolated tale. Students encountering this for the first time should note how specific and structured the account is, rather than a vague or arbitrary story.

What is known of its ritual life and key texts includes: Slavic mythology survives mostly through fragments recorded by early Christian chroniclers, later folklore collection, and comparative linguistic reconstruction, since the pre-Christian Slavic peoples left few if any surviving written religious texts of their own; Native American mythologies are extraordinarily diverse, reflecting hundreds of distinct nations and language groups across North America, each with its own specific traditions, ceremonies, and sacred narratives; Australian Aboriginal Dreamtime (or 'the Dreaming') is not simply a set of past myths but an ongoing spiritual framework connecting land, law, ceremony, and identity for Aboriginal peoples, maintained through art, ceremony, and songlines across tens of thousands of years of continuous culture. Read alongside the tradition's other elements, it forms part of a coherent worldview rather than an isolated tale. Students encountering this for the first time should note how specific and structured the account is, rather than a vague or arbitrary story. Comparative mythologists have long noted how this connects to patterns found in other, geographically distant traditions -- a useful reminder that human cultures have repeatedly reached for similar kinds of explanation. It is also worth asking what social or historical circumstance the account may reflect, since myth often encodes real concerns of the society that told it.

Modern culture continues to draw on it through: Baba Yaga and other Slavic mythological figures remain widely recognized across Eastern European literature, folklore, and popular culture today; Contemporary Native American communities across the United States and Canada continue to maintain, teach, and practice their specific tribal traditions and ceremonies today; Aboriginal Dreamtime art and storytelling remain a living, actively practiced tradition among Aboriginal Australian communities, and are increasingly presented in Australian museums and schools with the direct involvement of Aboriginal knowledge-holders. Comparative mythologists have long noted how this connects to patterns found in other, geographically distant traditions -- a useful reminder that human cultures have repeatedly reached for similar kinds of explanation. It is also worth asking what social or historical circumstance the account may reflect, since myth often encodes real concerns of the society that told it. This detail is among the better-documented parts of the tradition, thanks to surviving texts, inscriptions, or archaeological evidence. Later artists, writers, and, in some cases, entire religious movements have returned to this element repeatedly across the centuries.

No single module can cover every surviving story and variant of Other World Mythologies (Slavic, Native American, and Australian Aboriginal), but the elements above -- its deities, its account of origins, its heroes, its practice, and its legacy -- give a structured foundation for further study of one of the richest mythological traditions to survive from Eastern Europe, the Americas, and Australia.
